title: LLM APIs & Prompting
summary: Week 2. How LLMs work, calling Claude from Python, streaming, prompt engineering, structured output with Pydantic, tool calling, and retries and cost tracking. Project: a document extractor.

practice.title: Trim a conversation to fit the context window

practice.question: Your chatbot answers the first question well, but on the follow-up *"and what about the second one?"* it has no idea what you mean. What's the most likely cause?
options: The model's context window is full
Your app didn't resend the earlier messages with the new request
The model's weights were reset between requests
The model needs a higher temperature
practice.explanation: The API is **stateless**: each request stands alone and the model only sees what's in it. Follow-ups work only if your code sends the earlier turns again. Weights never change during inference, and one exchange is nowhere near filling a context window.

practice.question: Roughly how many tokens is a 2,000-word English document?
options: About 500
About 2,000
About 2,700
About 8,000
practice.explanation: A token is about ¾ of an English word (≈ 4 characters), so 2,000 words ≈ 2,000 ÷ 0.75 ≈ 2,700 tokens. Use `client.messages.count_tokens` when you need the exact number.

One turn of a chat with Claude

practice.question: A response comes back with `stop_reason == "max_tokens"`. What does that tell you?
options: You sent more input tokens than the model allows
The answer was cut off because it reached your `max_tokens` limit
You've used up your monthly token quota
The model finished its answer normally
practice.explanation: `max_tokens` caps the **output**. Hitting it means the reply stopped mid-answer. Raise the limit or ask for shorter output, and never ship a truncated answer as if it were complete.

practice.question: A call to `claude-sonnet-5-5` uses 10,000 input tokens and 2,000 output tokens. Sonnet 5.5 costs $2 per 1M input tokens and $10 per 1M output tokens. What does the call cost?
practice.explanation: Input: 10,000 · $2 / 1,000,000 = $0.02. Output: 2,000 · $10 / 1,000,000 = $0.02. Total **$0.04**. Output tokens are 5× the price of input here, so 2,000 output tokens cost as much as 10,000 input tokens.

practice.title: Wrap a stream in a generator

practice.question: What does switching from `messages.create` to `messages.stream` improve for a chat user?
options: The total time to generate the full answer
The time until the first words appear on screen
The cost per token
The accuracy of the answer
practice.explanation: The model generates at the same speed either way, and the price and output are the same. Streaming sends tokens as they're produced, so the user starts reading within a second or two instead of waiting for the whole answer.

practice.question: Why wrap a customer email in `<email>...</email>` tags inside your prompt?
options: The API requires XML for any text longer than a paragraph
It separates the data from your instructions, so the model can tell them apart and you can refer to it clearly
It makes the request cheaper because tags are free tokens
It stops the model from reading the email
practice.explanation: Tags are just text (they cost tokens like anything else) and the API doesn't require them. They make boundaries explicit: the model knows exactly what's data and what's instructions, which also makes it harder for text inside the email to be mistaken for instructions.

practice.question: Your prompt *"Summarise this report"* gives summaries that vary wildly in length and focus. What's the best first fix?
options: Run the same prompt several times and pick the best output
Say who the summary is for, what it must cover, the format, and a word limit
Switch to a bigger model
Add "Be accurate" to the end of the prompt
practice.explanation: The model fills every unstated decision itself, differently each time. Stating audience, content, format and length removes those choices. A bigger model given the same vague prompt still has to guess.

practice.title: Extract an invoice into a Pydantic model
Raw JSON schema output, with a retry

practice.question: You're extracting CVs. Many CVs don't list a phone number. Which field type should `phone` have in your Pydantic model?
options: `phone: str`
`phone: str | None`
`phone: int`
Leave `phone` out and parse it with a regex later
practice.explanation: A required `str` forces the model to produce *something*, and it may invent a plausible number. `str | None` lets it honestly return `null` when the CV doesn't say. Phone numbers aren't integers either: leading zeros and `+234` would be lost.

practice.title: Define a calculator tool, and don't trust its input

practice.question: Claude's reply contains two `tool_use` blocks (weather for Lagos and for Accra). How do you send the results back?
options: Two separate user messages, one `tool_result` each
One user message containing both `tool_result` blocks, each with its matching `tool_use_id`
One assistant message containing both results
Run only the first tool; Claude will ask for the second one next turn
practice.explanation: After appending the assistant turn, send **one** user message with a `tool_result` for every `tool_use` in that turn, matched by `tool_use_id`. Splitting them breaks the alternating roles and confuses the model.

practice.question: You set `"strict": True` on a `send_refund` tool. What does that guarantee?
options: The refund amount will be correct
The tool input matches your schema (types, required fields, no extra keys), but you still need to check the values make sense
The model will always call the tool
The tool can't be triggered by prompt injection
practice.explanation: Strict mode guarantees **shape**, not **safety**. The amount will be a number, but it could still be the wrong number or for the wrong customer. Validate meaning, scope access to the current user, and require human approval for anything irreversible.

practice.title: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter
Track spend per request and per day

practice.question: Which of these failed requests is worth retrying automatically?
options: 400 Bad Request
401 Unauthorized
529 Overloaded
404 Not Found
practice.explanation: 529 means the API is temporarily overloaded: wait and retry. 400, 401 and 404 mean something is wrong with your request, key or model name; the same request will fail again, so fix the code instead.

practice.question: Why add random jitter to exponential backoff delays?
options: It makes each retry cheaper
So many clients that failed at the same moment don't all retry at the same moment and fail together again
The API rejects retries that arrive at exact intervals
It lets you retry 400 errors safely
practice.explanation: Without jitter, every client that hit a rate limit at time *t* retries at exactly *t + 1 s*, *t + 3 s* and so on, creating synchronised spikes. Randomness spreads the retries out so they succeed.

project.title: Document extractor
checklist: Pydantic models for at least two document types (e.g. `Invoice` and `CV`), with descriptions, enums and optional fields
Single-document extraction with `messages.parse` and the text wrapped in XML tags
A business-rule check (e.g. line items add up to the total) that flags failures for review
Batch mode with `AsyncAnthropic`, `asyncio.gather` and a `Semaphore` limiting concurrency
Retries on 429/5xx with exponential backoff and jitter, and no retries on 400
One JSON file per document plus a summary file in `out/`
A cost report: documents, successes, failures, tokens, total and per-document cost
Offline tests with a fake client covering extraction, retries, concurrency and cost
README with setup, usage, sample output, and measured cost per document
Repo on GitHub with `.env` git-ignored and a `.env.example`
